title: 8 Best Wood Fillers in 2026: Match the Filler to the Damage
metaDescription: DAP Plastic Wood-X tops 8 wood fillers for most painted repairs. Picks by job: stained wood, rot, exterior trim, screw holes and fast nail-hole work.

intro:
The best wood filler for most repairs is DAP Plastic Wood-X with DryDex: a one-part latex that goes on pink and turns wood-toned when it is ready to sand, rated for interior and exterior use, paintable, stainable and cleaned up with water.

No single filler does every job, though. A cheap latex tub is perfect for nail holes and wrong for a quarter-inch-deep void, a joint that moves or a rotted window sill. Below are eight wood fillers matched to the damage they fix, followed by the questions that decide a good repair: filler versus putty versus caulk, staining, rot, large gaps, drying time and cold weather.
quickAnswer: For nail holes, dents and painted trim, buy DAP Plastic Wood-X. For stained wood, use Minwax Stainable or, indoors, Goodfilla. Rebuild rot with Abatron WoodEpox, make fast paint-grade exterior repairs with Minwax High Performance, and fix stripped screw holes with J-B Weld KwikWood. Fill anything deeper than about a quarter inch in layers, or switch to a two-part product.

sections.heading: Best Wood Filler: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Pick | Best for | Key spec |

| DAP Plastic Wood-X | Painted trim, doors, furniture | One-part latex, color-change DryDex |
| Minwax Stainable Wood Filler | Stained furniture, cabinets, floors | Takes oil- and water-based stain |
| Abatron WoodEpox | Rotted sills, jambs, columns | Two-part epoxy paste, no shrinkage |
| Minwax High Performance | Fast exterior repairs under paint | Two-part, sets fast |
| J-B Weld KwikWood | Stripped screw holes, quick fixes | Epoxy putty stick, drillable |
| Goodfilla Wood and Grain Filler | Furniture making, grain filling | Water-based, interior only |
| Gorilla All Purpose Wood Filler | Everyday patching on a budget | Acrylic, interior and exterior |
| FamoWood Latex Wood Filler | Many nail holes in one session | Fast-drying latex |

Start with the hole, then the finish. Shallow damage in wood that will be painted takes almost any one-part latex. Wood that will be stained needs a stainable formula in the right tone and a test on scrap. Damage outdoors, deep voids and rot need a two-part product that cures all the way through without shrinking.

A gap between two pieces that move, such as trim against a wall, is not a filler job at all. That calls for caulk.

sections.heading: The 8 Best Wood Fillers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The order reflects fit for purpose. For each filler, the ranking draws on the maker's label and specifications: chemistry, interior or exterior rating, set and sanding time, and whether it takes paint and stain, plus recurring themes in owner feedback. Figures a maker does not publish are left out.

### Best Overall: DAP Plastic Wood-X with DryDex

Plastic Wood-X wins because it handles the most common job, small and medium holes in trim, doors and furniture, with the least fuss. It goes on pink and shifts to a natural wood tone as it dries, so you never have to guess when it is ready for sandpaper. The paste spreads smoothly, stays put on vertical surfaces and sands to a crisp edge without clogging the paper.

DAP rates it for interior and exterior use and lists it as paintable and stainable, with water cleanup. Under paint it is about as foolproof as filler gets, and owners commonly report it holds up on exterior trim once primed and painted. Like any one-part latex, it is not structural; build anything deeper than a quarter inch in layers, and use a two-part product for rot or broken edges.

**Pros:** color change shows when it is ready to sand; smooth, non-sag paste; sands cleanly; interior and exterior rated; water cleanup.

**Cons:** deep holes need layers; not for rot or structural repairs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DAP+Plastic+Wood-X+DryDex&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Stained Projects: Minwax Stainable Wood Filler

Plenty of fillers say stainable; few take stain anywhere near the way the surrounding wood does. Minwax formulated this one to accept oil- and water-based stain more like real wood fibers, and owners commonly report it blends better than typical latex fillers on stained furniture, cabinets and floors.

It comes in several wood tones, so you can start close to your final color, which matters more than the stain itself. Minwax lists it for indoor and outdoor work, and it sands well and holds an edge on small breaks and gouges. Plan on a scrap test: fill, sand, stain beside the real wood and adjust before committing. It is not for large voids or rotted wood, and up close it will still read slightly differently from the grain.

**Pros:** formulated to accept stain more evenly; several wood tones; interior and exterior rated; sands to a clean edge.

**Cons:** still needs testing for a match; not for deep or structural repairs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Minwax+Stainable+Wood+Filler&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Rotted Wood: Abatron WoodEpox

Restoration carpenters use WoodEpox to rebuild rotted sills, door jambs, columns and trim that would otherwise be torn out. It is a two-part epoxy paste mixed in equal parts that cures into a hard, wood-like mass with essentially no shrinkage. Once cured, it can be sawn, planed, drilled, nailed, sanded and carved.

Abatron designs it to follow its LiquidWood consolidant, which soaks into softened fibers and hardens them before the paste goes on; together they form a waterproof repair bonded to sound wood. The trade-offs are cost, a working time that means mixing only what you can apply, and a learning curve. It is a paint-grade repair and will not take stain like wood. For exterior rot where the alternative is a new sill and a carpenter, it is the most capable product here.

**Pros:** rebuilds missing and rotted sections; no meaningful shrinkage; can be sawn, drilled and nailed when cured; waterproof; pairs with LiquidWood.

**Cons:** costs more than one-part fillers; mixing takes practice; paint-grade only.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Abatron+WoodEpox&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Fast Exterior Repair: Minwax High Performance Wood Filler

Minwax High Performance is a two-part filler, a can of filler plus a tube of hardener, mixed in small batches. It hardens quickly, so sanding and painting can follow much sooner than with a deep latex fill, and it does not shrink as it sets. That makes it a strong choice for exterior trim, broken corners and deep gouges on wood that will be painted.

Minwax pairs it with its Wood Hardener for softened wood, a lighter version of the consolidant-plus-filler method Abatron uses. The fast set is also its main drawback: mix only what you can apply in a few minutes, and work with ventilation because the odor is strong. It is paint-grade, so do not plan to stain it.

**Pros:** sets and sands fast; no shrinkage on deep fills; strong, weather-resistant repair; pairs with Minwax Wood Hardener.

**Cons:** short working time; strong odor; not stainable.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Minwax+High+Performance+Wood+Filler&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Quick Epoxy Fix: J-B Weld KwikWood

KwikWood is an epoxy stick you knead: slice off a piece, work it until the two parts blend to an even tan, press it into the damage and shape it. J-B Weld lists a set time of around a quarter hour and a cure time of about an hour, after which it can be drilled, sanded, painted and, to a degree, stained.

With nothing to measure, it excels at small, awkward repairs: a stripped cabinet screw hole, a chipped table leg, a broken door corner or a short stretch of damaged exterior trim. It is expensive per ounce over large areas, and its tan color shows through stain. For a quick, strong fix that holds a fastener and survives outdoors, it earns a spot in every toolbox.

**Pros:** no measuring; quick set and cure per the label; holds screws; works outdoors on small repairs.

**Cons:** costly for large areas; tan color shows through stain.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=J-B+Weld+KwikWood&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Woodworkers: Goodfilla Wood and Grain Filler

Goodfilla is aimed at furniture makers and flooring installers more than house painters. It is water-based, sold in a long list of species-matched colors, and can be thinned with water to act as a grain filler on open-pored woods like oak and ash, a job most wood fillers cannot do.

It also stays usable: the company says a batch that dries out can be revived with water, so less of it ends up in the trash. Owners commonly praise how easily it sands and how close the colors come, and it accepts stain and topcoats. Its limit is location: it is intended for interior use only, which rules out exterior trim and decks.

**Pros:** species-matched colors; doubles as grain filler when thinned; can be revived with water; sands easily; takes stain and topcoats.

**Cons:** interior use only; small containers cost more per ounce.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Goodfilla+wood+and+grain+filler&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget All-Purpose: Gorilla All Purpose Wood Filler

Gorilla's filler is an inexpensive acrylic for the jobs most homeowners face: nail holes, dents, gouges and small cracks inside and outside. Gorilla lists it as water resistant, shrink resistant and sandable, rated for interior and exterior use, with water cleanup. It spreads easily, holds on vertical surfaces and sands without much effort.

Gorilla markets it as paintable and stainable; treat the stain claim as you would for any latex-type filler and test on scrap. Like every one-part filler, it does best in shallow repairs, so build deep holes in layers. Owners commonly report it keeps well in the tub when the lid is sealed tightly.

**Pros:** low cost; interior and exterior rated; water resistant once dry; easy to spread and sand.

**Cons:** stain match is approximate; deep fills need layers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Gorilla+All+Purpose+Wood+Filler&tag=sktiger-20)

### Fastest Drying Latex: FamoWood Latex Wood Filler

FamoWood's latex filler is built for speed. Thin applications dry fast enough to sand in minutes rather than hours, which makes it a favorite of trim carpenters filling dozens of nail holes in one session. It comes in several wood tones, cleans up with water and is rated for interior and exterior use.

That speed cuts both ways. It skins over in the tub if the lid stays off, so scoop out a small amount and close the container between uses. It also shrinks a bit more than some rivals on deeper fills, so a second skim coat is common. On painted trim, cabinets and baseboard, the time savings are real.

**Pros:** dries and sands quickly in thin layers; several wood tones; water cleanup; interior and exterior rated.

**Cons:** skins in the tub if left open; deeper holes may need a second coat.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=FamoWood+latex+wood+filler&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Are the Different Types of Wood Filler?
sections.body:
There are five types: one-part latex or acrylic, one-part solvent-based, two-part polyester, two-part epoxy paste and epoxy putty sticks. Nearly every product on the shelf falls into one of them, so pick the type before you compare brands.

| Type | Shrinkage | Strength | Stain | Outdoors | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Latex or acrylic | Slight | Low | Fair | If primed and painted | Nail holes, dents, small cracks |
| Solvent one-part | Slight | Moderate | Fair | Yes | Harder-wearing small repairs |
| Two-part polyester | None | High | Poor | Yes | Exterior trim, broken corners |
| Two-part epoxy paste | None | Very high | Poor | Yes | Rot, rebuilding missing wood |
| Epoxy putty stick | None | High | Poor | Yes | Small strong fixes, screw holes |

### One-part latex or acrylic

The ready-to-use tubs most people know. They clean up with water and sand easily, but they harden by losing water, so they shrink slightly and work best in shallow holes. DAP Plastic Wood-X, Gorilla and FamoWood are in this group.

### Solvent-based one-part

These older formulas harden as their solvent evaporates. Most are tougher than latex, but they smell stronger and need solvent for cleanup, so ventilate. Water-based products have replaced many of them.

### Two-part polyester and epoxy

Two-part products harden by chemical reaction, so they cure through the whole depth without shrinking. Polyester fillers like Minwax High Performance set fast; epoxy pastes like Abatron WoodEpox are the heavy-duty choice for rot; putty sticks like KwikWood package epoxy for small jobs.

### What about steel-infused epoxy?

Steel-reinforced epoxies are formulated mainly for metal repair. For wood, a wood-specific epoxy such as WoodEpox or KwikWood is the better match, because it sands, shapes and takes fasteners much like the wood around it.

sections.heading: Wood Filler vs Wood Putty vs Caulk: What Is the Difference?
sections.body:
Filler dries hard, putty stays soft and caulk stays flexible, so each belongs in a different place. Mixing them up is behind a large share of failed repairs.

| Product | Cured state | Applied to | Sanded? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wood filler | Hard | Bare wood before finish | Yes | Holes and damage that do not move |
| Wood putty | Soft | Finished wood | No | Nail holes in stained work |
| Caulk or sealant | Flexible | Joints between pieces | No | Gaps that open and close |

### Filler

Filler goes onto bare wood, is sanded flush, then painted or finished. Because it is rigid, it belongs in damage inside a single piece: nail holes, gouges, dents and chipped edges.

### Putty

Putty is usually oil-based, comes in wood tones and goes into nail holes after the finish is on, mostly on stained trim and furniture. It is never sanded and should not go on bare wood that will be painted.

### Caulk

Caulk seals seams where two pieces shift against each other, such as trim against a wall or casing against siding. Rigid filler in one of those seams cracks with the first change of season.

### What fills a 1/8-inch gap in trim?

If the gap is a seam between two trim pieces or between trim and wall, use a paintable caulk, not filler. If it is a crack or open miter inside work that does not move, a latex filler like DAP Plastic Wood-X fills it in one pass. For outdoor seams, our [exterior caulk guide](/best-exterior-caulk/) has the picks.

sections.heading: Can You Stain Wood Filler?
sections.body:
Partly. Stainable filler absorbs some stain and darkens, but it almost never ends up matching the wood around it. Real wood has grain, uneven density and thirsty end grain, and a uniform paste cannot copy that.

### How to get closest

Choose a filler tone close to the final stained color, not the bare wood. Fill, let it dry, sand, then stain a scrap board that carries both wood and filler. If the patch comes out light, use a darker filler or mix a little stain or compatible tint into the filler; if it comes out dark, go lighter. Minwax Stainable and Goodfilla are the easiest to adjust this way.

### When to skip filler under stain

On trim, many finish carpenters stain and topcoat first, then press colored wax or oil-based putty that matches the finished color into the nail holes. On small holes that disappears far better than any stainable filler.

### Old furniture and heirlooms

On a century-old rocking chair or similar stained piece, use the smallest possible patch of Minwax Stainable or Goodfilla in a matched tone, test on a hidden spot, and fix loose joints with glue rather than filler.

### Two-part fillers

Two-part polyester and epoxy fillers do not take stain in any meaningful way. On stained exterior wood like a cedar fence, you either accept a visible repair or replace the board. For decks and siding under semi-transparent stain, our [deck stain reviews](/best-deck-stain-reviews/) cover the options.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Wood Filler for Exterior and Rotted Wood?
sections.body:
For small holes outdoors, an exterior-rated latex like DAP Plastic Wood-X works once primed and painted. Anything larger on exterior trim, siding or a door is better served by a two-part product like Minwax High Performance, and rot needs a consolidant followed by an epoxy such as Abatron WoodEpox.

### Repairing rot in four steps

1. **Remove the rot.** Cut out every fiber soft enough to dent with a fingernail or awl, using a chisel, rasp or oscillating tool.
2. **Let it dry.** Moisture trapped under epoxy makes the repair fail.
3. **Consolidate.** Soak the remaining fibers with Abatron LiquidWood or Minwax Wood Hardener so they harden.
4. **Rebuild.** Overfill slightly with a two-part filler, shape it close to the profile while workable, then sand or plane flush, prime and paint once cured.

Done properly, a repair like this can last as long as the wood around it. Done over damp, punky wood, it pops loose within a year. Ventilate when mixing two-part products and wear gloves with uncured epoxy.

### When to replace instead

Replacement usually wins when rot runs through most of the board's thickness, touches a structural member, or covers more than about a third of a trim piece.

### Fix the water first

Rot returns if the water does. At a sill, the cause is often failed caulk or a missing drip cap; at a jamb, splashback or a missing door sweep. Seal the joints afterward and keep the wood covered with paint or a finish from our [exterior wood sealer guide](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/).

### Is there a flexible exterior wood filler?

Rigid fillers do not flex. Where wood moves seasonally, as at board ends and seams, use an exterior sealant and keep filler for damage within a single board.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Wood Filler for Large Gaps?
sections.body:
For large gaps and deep holes, use a two-part product: Minwax High Performance for fast paint-grade fills, Abatron WoodEpox for big or rotted voids. They cure through their full depth without shrinking, which one-part latex cannot do.

### Why latex fails in deep holes

A thick plug of one-part latex forms a dry crust over a wet center. When the center finally dries, it shrinks and cracks. If you must use latex, keep each layer to about a quarter inch, let it dry all the way through, then add the next.

### Wood filler with structural strength

No filler restores structural strength to a joist, stair tread, railing post or anything else that carries load. Epoxies like WoodEpox are strong enough to saw, plane and nail, but they are surface and trim repairs. Load-bearing damage calls for replacement or reinforcement, and anything that holds weight overhead or underfoot should be properly assessed.

### Dutchman patches

For a large hole in stained wood where any filler would show, a patch of matching wood glued into a squared-up recess often looks better than filler. It is a little more work and nearly invisible when the grain is aligned.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply and Sand Wood Filler?
sections.body:
Clean the hole, press filler in with a slight crown, build deep holes in layers, sand flat once fully dry and prime before painting. The order matters more than the brand.

### Clean and shape the hole

Pick out loose fibers, dust and old finish, since filler only bonds to sound wood. For bigger damage, square the edges with a chisel so the filler has firm walls to lock against. Wipe dust away with a barely damp rag and let it dry.

### Press, do not spread

Force filler into the hole with a flexible putty knife, then scrape across at a low angle to remove most of the excess. Leave a slight crown, because one-part fillers shrink a little. A fill that sits flush or low will need a second coat.

### Sand once fully dry

On flat work, start with 120-grit on a sanding block so the patch ends up level rather than dished, then move to 180 or 220. On molded trim, wrap paper around a dowel or profile block. Shine a raking light across the surface to find pinholes and low spots, and fill them before moving on.

### Prime before paint

Wood and filler absorb paint at different rates, so an unprimed patch flashes through the topcoat as a dull or glossy spot. Spot-prime each repair, using a bonding primer outdoors. If you are refinishing a lot of trim or cabinets after the repairs, a [paint sprayer](/best-paint-sprayer/) gives the most even finish over filled areas.

sections.heading: How Long Does Wood Filler Take to Dry, and Does It Work in Cold Weather?
sections.body:
Wood filler takes anywhere from about 15 minutes for a thin latex skim to a day for a two-part epoxy paste, depending on type, depth and temperature. The label always wins over these typical ranges.

| Filler and depth | Typical time before sanding |
| --- | --- |
| Thin latex fill | 15-60 minutes |
| Deep latex fill | 2-8 hours |
| Two-part polyester | 20-30 minutes |
| Two-part epoxy paste | Hours to a day |

### Latex

Latex dries as its water evaporates, so depth, temperature and humidity set the pace. A skim on a nail hole may be ready in 15 minutes; a deep fill packed in one go can stay soft at the core. Color-change formulas like DAP Plastic Wood-X tell you when they are dry.

### Two-part products

Two-part fillers cure by chemical reaction, so the center cures along with the surface. Polyester fillers can often be sanded within half an hour; epoxy pastes need several hours to overnight.

### What wood fillers work in 40-degree temps?

Check the minimum application temperature on the label before working in the cold. Around 40 degrees, water-based fillers dry very slowly and may be below the label minimum, and freezing ruins them in the tub. Cold also slows every two-part product considerably. Warm the work area and the wood if you can, bring the filler indoors overnight, or move the job to a warmer day.

### Fill, caulk, then paint

If the trim also needs caulk, fill, sand and prime first, caulk second, and paint only once the sealant label says it is ready.

sections.heading: Goodfilla vs Minwax vs FamoWood: Which Is Better?
sections.body:
Goodfilla is better for indoor furniture and grain filling, Minwax Stainable is better for stained work that may go outdoors, and FamoWood is better for speed on painted trim. They solve different problems, so the right answer depends on the job.

### Goodfilla vs Minwax Stainable

Both are made to take stain. Goodfilla offers species-matched colors, thins with water into a grain filler for oak and ash, and can be revived with water if it dries out, but it is interior only. Minwax Stainable comes in several wood tones and is rated for indoor and outdoor work. For a dining table in red oak, Goodfilla is the stronger choice; for a stained exterior door, Minwax.

### Goodfilla vs FamoWood

FamoWood dries fast enough to sand within minutes in thin layers and is rated inside and out, which suits a trim carpenter filling dozens of nail holes before paint. Goodfilla works more slowly but blends better under stain and fills grain. Pick FamoWood for painted production work and Goodfilla for furniture.

### Is there a FamoWood substitute?

If FamoWood is not on the shelf, DAP Plastic Wood-X or Gorilla All Purpose cover the same painted nail-hole work, trading a little drying speed for a smooth, easy-sanding paste.

sections.heading: Can You Screw or Nail Into Wood Filler?
sections.body:
Not into one-part latex, but a fully cured epoxy can take a screw through a pilot hole. Latex and acrylic fillers crumble when a screw turns in them, so they are the wrong fix for a stripped hinge screw.

### Epoxy for fasteners

Pack the stripped hole with J-B Weld KwikWood or Abatron WoodEpox, wait for the full cure, then drill a pilot hole sized for the screw and drive it in. Both makers describe their products as drillable and able to hold fasteners once cured.

### Heavily loaded screws

For a door hinge or railing bracket, the old method still holds best: glue a hardwood dowel, or a few wooden toothpicks, into the hole, trim flush once dry and drill a fresh pilot.

### Nails

Driving a nail through most fillers cracks them, though cured epoxy paste generally takes a nail through a predrilled hole. If you know the repair will need fastening, choose epoxy or bed a wood block or dowel in the repair to nail into later. Before you drill into walls around trim, a [stud finder](/best-stud-finder/) helps you hit solid framing.

mistakes.title: Believing the word stainable
mistakes.body: Stainable means the patch absorbs some color, not that it disappears into the grain. Start with a filler tone near the finished color, test on scrap with the real stain, and consider colored putty after finishing for small holes.

mistakes.title: Filling a deep hole in one pass
mistakes.body: A thick plug of one-part latex skins over while the core stays wet, then shrinks and cracks. Build in layers of about a quarter inch, letting each dry, or use a two-part product that cures through without shrinking.

mistakes.title: Using filler in a joint that moves
mistakes.body: Rigid filler between trim and wall, or casing and siding, cracks as soon as humidity and temperature shift the pieces. Seal moving joints with flexible caulk and keep filler for damage inside one piece of wood.

mistakes.title: Patching over rot without removing it
mistakes.body: Filler over soft, rotted wood has nothing sound to grip and traps moisture, so the patch pops loose while the rot spreads. Dig out every soft fiber, dry the area, consolidate, rebuild with epoxy and stop the water source.

mistakes.title: Leaving exterior filler unprimed
mistakes.body: Exterior latex filler still degrades when sun and rain hit it bare, and it absorbs paint differently from wood. Spot-prime every repair with a bonding primer, paint the whole surface, and inspect outdoor patches each spring.

faqs.q: What is the best wood filler?
faqs.a: DAP Plastic Wood-X with DryDex is the best wood filler for most repairs. It is a one-part latex rated for interior and exterior use, it changes color when ready to sand, and it is paintable and stainable with water cleanup. For rot, use Abatron WoodEpox; for stained furniture, Minwax Stainable or Goodfilla; for stripped screw holes, J-B Weld KwikWood.

faqs.q: What is the best wood filler for large gaps?
faqs.a: A two-part filler is best for large gaps: Minwax High Performance for fast paint-grade repairs or Abatron WoodEpox for big and rotted voids. Both cure through their full depth without shrinking. One-part latex cracks in deep fills unless you build it in layers of about a quarter inch, letting each layer dry completely.

faqs.q: Which is better, Goodfilla or FamoWood filler?
faqs.a: Goodfilla is better for stained indoor furniture and grain filling, and FamoWood is better for fast work on painted trim. Goodfilla offers species-matched colors and can be revived with water but is interior only. FamoWood dries fast enough to sand in minutes in thin layers and is rated for interior and exterior use.

faqs.q: Is there a wood filler with structural strength?
faqs.a: No wood filler restores structural strength to a load-bearing part. Epoxies such as Abatron WoodEpox and J-B Weld KwikWood cure hard enough to saw, drill and hold screws, which makes them the strongest repairs here, but they are for trim, sills and furniture. Joists, stair treads and railing posts need replacement or reinforcement.

faqs.q: What wood fillers work in 40 degree temps?
faqs.a: Check each label's minimum application temperature first, because water-based fillers dry very slowly in the cold, 40 degrees may be below the listed minimum, and freezing ruins them. Two-part products also cure much more slowly when it is cool. Warm the work area and the wood if you can, keep the filler indoors until use, or wait for a warmer day.

faqs.q: Is wood putty the same as wood filler?
faqs.a: No. Wood filler hardens, goes onto bare wood, is sanded flush and then painted or finished. Wood putty stays soft, is usually oil-based and fills nail holes after the finish is already on, mostly on stained trim and furniture. Putty is never sanded and should not be used on bare wood that will be painted.

faqs.q: Is solvent based wood filler better than latex?
faqs.a: Solvent-based filler is usually tougher than latex and handles harder-wearing small repairs, but it smells stronger and needs solvent for cleanup. Latex fillers like DAP Plastic Wood-X sand easily, clean up with water and are good enough for most painted repairs. For deep or exterior damage, a two-part filler beats both.

bottomLine: Match the filler to the damage and almost any product here does its job. DAP Plastic Wood-X is the best everyday wood filler for nail holes, dents and painted trim. Use Minwax Stainable or Goodfilla when stain goes on top, Minwax High Performance for fast exterior repairs, Abatron WoodEpox with a consolidant for rot, and J-B Weld KwikWood for stripped screw holes. Build deep fills in layers or switch to two-part, keep caulk in the joints that move, test stain on scrap, and prime every patch before you paint.
